annotations.text:
A · TWO-SIDED LEDGER — the axis is DENSITY

Keep one document; make its two sides legible. The 1px rule at track 7 was already there — what it never had was a NAME on each side of it. The shop's three columns rest at ink-600 and come to full ink only on the line you are working, so reading down the client's prices is never interrupted by a cost.

New here: a floor under the price you are editing ("holds 10% at 105,556"), a keep-meter with your floor notched on it, a goods subtotal, and a 3-to-settle strip whose buttons act on the rows above.

TRADEOFF: still ten columns. Fastest for a rep who already knows the screen, most to read for one who doesn't.

B · SHEET & ANSWER — the axis is CLARITY  (my recommendation)

Split the two conversations. Left is the CLIENT'S sheet: five columns, nothing else — no cost, no supplier, no margin. It is the paper they receive, and you can turn the laptop round. Right is the SHOP'S answer to the line you are on, which finally has room to carry a real supplier comparison (three ranked, with what the book knows) instead of a 130px hint.

New here: the price floor, the margin measured against YOUR floor and against what this client usually pays, the three suppliers ranked at this quantity, and a foot that says when the prices were taken and how long the quote holds.

TRADEOFF: per-line cost needs a selection (arrow keys / click). You trade a glance for a keystroke — and get a client-facing document and 400px of reasoning for it.

C · DEAL FIRST — the axis is LEVERAGE

Invert the screen. The money reads at the TOP, where the eye lands; the acts stay at the FOOT, where the hands are. A deal band carries who it is with, what they pay, and what is left of it, with the floor stated in words. Under it, ONE decision at a time — a list of three decisions is a reason to make none — with the other two named behind a Next. Entry is a command bar that holds the caret when the screen opens.

New here: everything in B's intelligence, plus the decision queue and always-on entry.

TRADEOFF: it drops the house page-header component this screen shares with forty other screens, and spends ~200px before the first line. The most to learn, and the only one that answers "how low can I go" before you are asked.

820px is a SWITCH, not a reflow. B's two columns become the phone's two tabs — the client's sheet, and the shop's answer behind a dot when it has something to say. 15px body, 44px steppers, the name holds its width and the meta beside it is what truncates, and the foot carries the one figure said down the phone plus the two acts. Nothing sends itself.
